title: One Condition Apart
blurb: Ten pairs of near-identical tenants, each separated by a single flipped setting. Read both scenes, spot the one variable that moved, and sort each one to the outcome it actually produces.
source: Microsoft Learn: Conditional Access overview, policy components, grant and session controls, deployment planning; Entra ID Protection overview; PIM assignment, activation and planning; OAuth permissions and consent; managed identities for Azure resources · SC-500 outline 1.1

pairs.dimension: a requirement that must be met before the door opens vs a limit imposed on the session once the user is already inside

a.text: At a Leeds law firm, a paralegal opening the case-files SharePoint site on her home laptop is stopped at sign-in until the laptop reports as Intune compliant. Non-compliant machines never reach the site at all.
a.why: Requiring a compliant device is a grant control, evaluated in the enforcement phase before any token for the resource is issued, so a failed check ends the sign-in. The session side is wrong because session controls never decide whether access happens, only how constrained it is after it has already been granted.
a.citation: Learn: Conditional Access grant controls · outline 1.1

b.text: At the same Leeds firm, a paralegal on the same home laptop does reach the case-files SharePoint site, but the browser view is read-only with downloading and printing switched off because the machine is unmanaged.
b.why: App enforced restrictions hand device state to SharePoint Online so the app itself serves a cut-down experience, which is a limit applied inside a session that has already been granted. It is not a grant control because nothing blocked the sign-in; access succeeded and only the richness of the session changed.
b.citation: Learn: Conditional Access session controls · outline 1.1

pairs.citation: Learn: Conditional Access grant and session controls · outline 1.1

pairs.dimension: a policy that only records what it would have done vs the same policy actually deciding the sign-in

a.text: A credit union builds a policy that blocks sign-ins to its loan-origination app from outside the United Kingdom, then leaves it observing for a week before it is allowed to decide anything. That night a contractor in Lisbon reaches the app without trouble, and next morning the analyst opens that sign-in event and finds the policy listed with the verdict it would have reached.
a.why: A policy in this state still joins the first phase of evaluation, where session details are gathered, and its would-be result is written to the sign-in log, but enforcement is skipped, so the contractor's session was never touched. It is not the enabled state because an enabled block would have terminated that sign-in rather than merely recording a verdict.
a.citation: Learn: plan a Conditional Access deployment · outline 1.1

b.text: A week later the same credit union switches that same location policy to On. The Lisbon contractor's next attempt on the loan-origination app fails outright, and the sign-in event names the policy as the reason the attempt did not complete.
b.why: Once enabled, the policy reaches the enforcement phase, and a block control ends evaluation immediately, so the sign-in from the excluded country is refused. Report-only is wrong here because the outcome changed the sign-in itself rather than only appearing as a simulated result in the log.
b.citation: Learn: Conditional Access policy components · outline 1.1

pairs.citation: Learn: Conditional Access policy components and deployment planning · outline 1.1

pairs.dimension: risk attached to one authentication attempt vs risk attached to the account itself

a.text: A hospital data analyst signs in from Manchester at 09:00 and again from an anonymising proxy in another continent at 09:40. ID Protection scores that second attempt as probably not coming from the real account holder, and the tenant policy makes her satisfy multifactor authentication before the session continues.
a.why: Sign-in risk is calculated in real time for a single authentication event and expresses how likely that particular request is not the genuine owner, which is exactly what impossible travel through an anonymous IP produces. User risk is wrong because nothing here says the account itself is believed compromised beyond this one attempt.
a.citation: Learn: Conditional Access conditions and ID Protection overview · outline 1.1

b.text: The same hospital analyst signs in normally from her usual Manchester desk, but her work address and password have turned up in a credentials dump ID Protection ingested overnight. The tenant policy makes her complete a secure password change before she can carry on.
b.why: Leaked credentials attach a compromise likelihood to the identity itself, which persists across sessions until it is remediated, so the correct answer is the account-level signal. It is not sign-in risk because the sign-in in front of us looks entirely ordinary; the risk was carried in by the account, and the Require password change control is only usable with the user risk condition.
b.citation: Learn: Conditional Access grant controls and ID Protection overview · outline 1.1

pairs.citation: Learn: Conditional Access conditions, grant controls, ID Protection overview · outline 1.1

pairs.dimension: privilege the person must switch on before use vs privilege they simply hold

a.text: A retail platform engineer needs Key Vault Contributor on the payments subscription. Each time she starts release work she opens Privileged Identity Management, requests the role for four hours, types a change-ticket justification, and waits for her manager to approve before the permission appears.
a.why: An eligible assignment gives the person the potential to hold the role, and PIM makes them take an action to use it, which can include a multifactor check, a justification and approval. Active is wrong because an active holder does nothing at all to start using the role, so no request, approval or expiry would appear.
a.citation: Learn: assign Azure resource roles in PIM · outline 1.1

b.text: Her colleague on the same retail payments subscription also has Key Vault Contributor, but he simply opens the portal and edits secrets straight away. Nothing prompts him, nothing is logged as an activation, and the rights sit on his account overnight and at weekends.
b.why: An active assignment is usable the moment it exists, with no activation step in front of it, which is why the standing rights persist between tasks. It is not eligible because eligibility never grants anything until the holder activates it, and every activation would leave an audit entry with the reason given.
b.citation: Learn: assign Azure resource roles in PIM · outline 1.1

pairs.dimension: an assignment with no end date vs the same assignment bounded by start and end times

a.text: A university names its long-serving directory lead as eligible for Exchange Recipient Administrator. The Privileged Identity Management record carries no expiry, so two years later she can still request the role whenever a mailbox migration comes up.
a.why: A permanent assignment has no expiration and suits staff who repeatedly need the role, which is why the eligibility survives untouched for years. Time-bound is wrong because a bounded record would have lapsed on its end date and the lead would have to ask for a renewal or extension.
a.citation: Learn: assign Microsoft Entra roles in PIM · outline 1.1

b.text: The same university makes a six-week migration contractor eligible for Exchange Recipient Administrator, entering a start date on his first Monday and an end date the Friday his statement of work closes. After that Friday his requests to activate are refused.
b.why: Time-bound assignments are the option for temporary or contract staff whose finish date is known, and eligibility only exists between the two dates, so activation stops working afterwards. It is not permanent because a permanent record would leave the contractor able to elevate long after the engagement ended.
b.citation: Learn: assign Microsoft Entra roles in PIM · outline 1.1

pairs.dimension: proving a second factor about the person vs proving the machine is managed and healthy
buckets: Require device to be marked as compliant

a.text: A courier firm dispatcher opens Outlook on his own unenrolled Android phone, approves the number-match prompt in Microsoft Authenticator, and his mail loads. Nobody ever asks about the phone itself.
a.why: The control here is satisfied by a second proof from the human being, so an unmanaged personal handset is perfectly acceptable once the prompt is answered. The compliance control is wrong because it would have examined the device record in Intune, and this phone has none.
a.citation: Learn: Conditional Access grant controls · outline 1.1

b.text: A second courier firm dispatcher opens Outlook on his own unenrolled Android phone and also approves the Authenticator prompt, yet mail never loads. The sign-in log says the device is not recognised as meeting policy, and enrolling the handset in Intune is what finally lets him in.
b.answer: Require device to be marked as compliant
b.why: This control depends on a management system such as Intune reporting device state back to Entra ID, and a device has to be registered in Entra ID before it can be marked compliant at all, so an unenrolled personal handset fails no matter how well the human authenticates. Requiring multifactor authentication is wrong because he already answered that challenge and was still refused.
b.citation: Learn: Conditional Access grant controls · outline 1.1

pairs.citation: Learn: Conditional Access grant controls · outline 1.1

pairs.dimension: any accepted second factor vs a named set of methods the policy will settle for

a.text: An engineering consultancy protects its Azure management portal so that admins must complete a second factor. A network lead elevates from a hotel and gets in by typing a code texted to his mobile.
a.why: The plain multifactor control asks only that Entra multifactor authentication be completed, so whichever registered method the person reaches for satisfies it, including a text message code. Authentication strength is wrong because a strength requirement would have named which methods count and refused the weaker one.
a.citation: Learn: Conditional Access grant controls · outline 1.1

b.text: A second engineering consultancy protects its Azure management portal the same way, but when its network lead elevates from a hotel the text-message code is not offered at all. He is told to tap his security key, and only the passkey lets him through.
b.why: Authentication strengths, built in or custom and defined under Authentication methods in the Entra admin center, let the policy insist on a specific combination such as phishing-resistant credentials, which is why the text code was never presented. The plain multifactor control is wrong because it would have happily accepted that text code as a valid second factor.
b.citation: Learn: Conditional Access grant controls and authentication methods policy · outline 1.1

pairs.citation: Learn: Conditional Access grant controls, authentication strengths · outline 1.1

pairs.dimension: an app acting for a signed-in person vs an app acting entirely as itself

a.text: A charity uses a document-search web app. A fundraiser signs in to it, the app calls Microsoft Graph carrying her identity, and search results only ever include the files she could open herself in SharePoint.
a.why: Delegated permissions, also called scopes, let the client call an API using the identity of whoever signed in, and both the app and the person must be authorised, so the app can never see beyond that user's own reach. Application permission is wrong because an app-only grant would ignore the fundraiser's own access boundary entirely.
a.citation: Learn: OAuth permissions and consent · outline 1.1

b.text: The same charity also runs an overnight compliance scanner with nobody signed in. It authenticates as itself, calls Microsoft Graph, and its report lists documents from every team site in the tenant, including ones no member of the IT team can open.
b.why: Application permissions are app roles used in app-only access with no user present, so the client reaches all data the permission covers across the tenant, and generally only an administrator or the resource service principal owner can consent to them. Delegated is wrong because there is no signed-in identity to scope the request down to.
b.citation: Learn: OAuth permissions and consent · outline 1.1

pairs.citation: Learn: OAuth permissions and consent · outline 1.1

pairs.dimension: a permission a member of staff may approve themselves vs one only an administrator can approve

a.text: A marketing manager at an insurer signs up for a design tool that asks to read her own profile and her own calendar. She sees the permissions screen, presses Accept, and the tool starts working immediately without IT hearing about it.
a.why: Where the tenant's consent settings leave user consent switched on, a member can approve for herself any permission that carries no administrator requirement, which is what these low-privilege delegated scopes over her own mailbox and profile are. Administrator consent is wrong because nothing in this request reaches beyond the manager's own mailbox and profile.
a.citation: Learn: configure user consent settings · outline 1.1

b.text: The same insurer's marketing manager then tries a reporting add-in that asks to read files across the whole organisation. The Accept button is not hers to press, so she fills in a justification box and her request lands in a queue for a reviewer to approve.
b.why: Tenant-wide permissions such as reading all files, and other high-privilege scopes, can only be granted by an administrator, and the admin consent workflow is what turns the dead end into a reviewable request. User consent is wrong because permitting members to grant this class of permission would hand a third-party app organisation-wide data reach on one person's decision.
b.citation: Learn: configure user consent settings and admin consent workflow · outline 1.1

pairs.citation: Learn: OAuth permissions, user consent settings · outline 1.1

pairs.dimension: an identity whose life is tied to one resource vs an identity that exists in its own right

a.text: A logistics team turns on a managed identity directly on the route-planning virtual machine and grants it reader rights on one storage account. When the machine is decommissioned in the spring rebuild, the identity and its role assignment disappear with it.
a.why: This kind of identity is created on and bound to a single Azure resource, cannot be shared with another, and is removed when the resource is deleted, which is exactly the lifecycle described. The user-assigned side is wrong because a standalone identity would have outlived the virtual machine and kept its role assignment.
a.citation: Learn: managed identities for Azure resources · outline 1.1

b.text: The same logistics team later creates the identity first, as its own Azure resource with the storage rights already in place, then attaches it to the rebuilt route-planning virtual machine and to two batch workers that do the same job. Rebuilding any of the three leaves the identity and its permissions untouched.
b.why: A standalone managed identity is provisioned independently of compute, can be attached to several resources at once, and survives their deletion, so permissions can be prepared before the workloads exist. It is not system-assigned because that type can only ever be associated with the one resource it was enabled on and vanishes with it.
b.citation: Learn: managed identities for Azure resources · outline 1.1

pairs.citation: Learn: managed identities for Azure resources · outline 1.1
